name: The Hydra
description: The many-headed water serpent of Lerna that grew two heads for every one cut off

debut.title: Hesiod's Theogony
debut.creator: Hesiod
debut.era: Theogony, around 700 BCE; the labour is told in full by Apollodorus

legend: The Hydra lived in the swamp at Lerna, south of Argos, where the springs were said to be bottomless, and was raised by the goddess Hera out of spite for Heracles. Hesiod, around 700 BCE, makes it a child of Typhon and Echidna and tells how Heracles and his nephew Iolaus destroyed it, but gives no number of heads; the poet Alcaeus settled on nine a century later, and others went as high as fifty. Killing it was the second of the twelve labours. Apollodorus tells the version everyone knows: Heracles forced the Hydra out of its lair with burning arrows, grabbed it, and found that every time he smashed a head with his club two grew in its place, while Hera sent an enormous crab to nip at his feet. He crushed the crab, which Hera placed among the stars as Cancer, and called Iolaus, who burned each neck stump with a torch as his uncle lopped the head off. The middle head was immortal, so Heracles buried it under a heavy rock by the road and dipped his arrows in the creature's venomous gall. Those arrows later killed the centaur Nessus, whose poisoned blood would in turn kill Heracles himself. Eurystheus refused to count the labour because Iolaus had helped. Linnaeus named the tiny freshwater polyp Hydra in 1758 because it regrows from pieces, the largest of the 88 constellations is the Hydra, and a moon of Pluto discovered in 2005 was named after it too.

myths.claim: Two heads grew back for every one that was cut off.
myths.explanation: That is what Apollodorus says, and Ovid has Hercules remember the monster growing stronger with every wound. Hesiod, the oldest source, does not mention regrowing heads at all.
His nephew Iolaus cauterised each neck with a burning torch so that the heads could not grow back, which is why Eurystheus refused to count the labour.

myths.claim: The Hydra's venom eventually killed Heracles.
myths.explanation: He dipped his arrows in its gall and later shot the centaur Nessus with one. Nessus's poisoned blood, smeared on a shirt, burned Heracles to death years afterwards.

myths.claim: Hera sent a crab to help the Hydra.
myths.explanation: The crab nipped at Heracles' feet until he crushed it. Hera put it in the sky as the constellation Cancer.

myths.claim: The Hydra had nine heads in every ancient source.
myths.explanation: Hesiod gives no number, Alcaeus nine, and later poets fifty or more. Nine, with one immortal, is Apollodorus's count and the one that stuck.

quotes.text: Now the hydra had a huge body, with nine heads, eight mortal, but the middle one immortal.
quotes.speaker: Apollodorus
quotes.source: The Library, book 2, Sir James Frazer's 1921 translation

quotes.text: Nor could he effect anything by smashing its heads with his club, for as fast as one head was smashed there grew up two.
quotes.speaker: Apollodorus, on Heracles
quotes.source: The Library, book 2, Sir James Frazer's 1921 translation

powers: Two new heads for every one lost
One head that cannot die at all
A goddess on its side, and a crab
legacy: Ray Harryhausen's seven-headed Hydra guarding the Golden Fleece in Jason and the Argonauts (1963)
Disney's Hercules (1997), where the Hydra is the young hero's first big fight
HYDRA, the Marvel Comics organisation whose motto is 'cut off one head, two more shall take its place'
Percy Jackson: Sea of Monsters (2013), with a Hydra in a doughnut shop
The constellation Hydra, the largest of the 88, and Pluto's moon Hydra, found in 2005

hostIntro: Tonight's guest has more heads than our camera crew, and losing one only improves its mood. If you brought a sword, you brought the wrong thing.
